title: Reviewing your own writing
keyIdea: Reviewing your own writing means asking two kinds of question: is it correct, and does it work? Correct means spelling, capital letters and punctuation. Working means it has the intended effect on your reader. Read your draft as the reader, cut or change any line that breaks the effect, show feelings instead of telling them, order sentences so the best bit lands at the right moment, and check the draft against its success criteria.

kid: When you finish a draft, it is easy to check only the spelling. But a story with perfect spelling can still be boring. So ask two questions. Is it correct? And does it work?

Every piece of writing has a goal. You might want your reader to feel scared, to laugh, or to agree with you. That goal is the effect. To check it, read your draft as if you were the reader. Where do you feel it? Where does the feeling drop?

Some lines break the effect. A nice cheese sandwich in the middle of a ghost story makes the reader relax. Cut it or change it. Lines that tell a feeling, like I was scared, are weak too. Show it instead: My knees shook and I could not breathe.

Order matters. A surprise works best at the end, after the reader has wondered. Last, check your success criteria, the list of what your piece must do. A letter asking for a class pet needs reasons, not just please.
adult: The English national curriculum asks pupils in Years 3 and 4 to evaluate and edit by assessing the effectiveness of their own and others' writing and suggesting improvements. In Years 5 and 6 they propose changes to vocabulary, grammar and punctuation to enhance effects and clarify meaning. US Common Core W.3.5 and W.4.5 ask pupils to strengthen writing by planning, revising and editing.

Reviewing for effect is different from proof-reading. Proof-reading checks spelling, punctuation and grammar. Reviewing asks whether the text meets its purpose for its audience. Children do this best when the goal is named first, for example to scare the reader, and when they reread aloud as the reader would.

Common mistakes: stopping once the spelling is right; adding intensifiers such as very, very scared, which still tells rather than shows; keeping a line because it is true even when it breaks the mood; giving the ending away in the first sentence; and checking success criteria by ticking them without finding the line that meets each one.
Try one question at a time. Ask: where would my reader feel it most, and where would they stop feeling it? Praise a specific change, such as a cut line or a moved sentence, more than a longer draft.

familyTip: Ask your child to read a story or card they wrote aloud to you. Before they start, agree the goal, such as make Grandma laugh. Afterwards, ask: where did I laugh, and where did I stop? Let them change just one line.

visual.caption: Does each question check if it is correct, or if it works on the reader? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Does each sentence end with a full stop?
Will my reader want to turn the page?
Does the ending surprise my reader?
Would my reader laugh at this joke?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort correct-or-works questions, read drafts as the reader, show not tell, save the surprise, and check a letter against success criteria.

practice.prompt: Zara checked her story and found {n} spelling slips. She fixed them all. What should she ask next?
choices: Does my story have the effect I want on the reader?
practice.hint: Correct is one question. What is the other one?
practice.explain: Fixing all {n} slips makes it correct. Now she should read it as the reader and ask if it works.

practice.prompt: Which line shows, not tells, that Ben was excited?
choices: Ben bounced on his toes and grinned
practice.hint: Showing tells you what Ben did, so you can work out the feeling.
practice.explain: Bouncing and grinning let the reader see the excitement. Very, very excited and excited and happy still tell.

practice.prompt: A scary story has {n} lines. One says: "We had a lovely picnic in the sun." What should the writer do?
choices: Cut or change it, because it breaks the scary effect
Keep it, because every line counts
practice.hint: Does a sunny picnic make the reader feel scared or relaxed?
practice.explain: A lovely picnic makes the reader relax. Out of the {n} lines, this one breaks the effect, so cut it or change it.

practice.prompt: A joke story tells the funny ending in the first line. What is the best fix?
choices: Move the funny bit to the end
practice.hint: When does a surprise work best: before or after the reader has wondered?
practice.explain: A surprise or punchline works best at the end, so the reader builds up to it. Full stops and long words do not fix the order.

pool.prompt: Which question checks if your writing works?
choices: Will my reader want to read on?
pool.hint: One question is about the reader. The others are about rules.
pool.explain: Wanting to read on is about the effect on the reader. Spelling and capitals check if it is correct.

pool.prompt: What is the effect of a piece of writing?
choices: How it makes the reader feel or think
pool.hint: Think about the reader, not the page.
pool.explain: The effect is what the writing does to the reader, such as making them scared, laugh or agree.

pool.prompt: Max wants a letter to make the head say yes to a pet. It has {n} lines, but none says why. What is missing?
choices: A reason it would help the class
pool.hint: What would persuade the head to say yes?
pool.explain: All {n} lines ask, but none gives a reason. A reason, such as it would teach us to care for animals, makes it work.

pool.prompt: How should you check your draft for its effect?
choices: Read it as if you were the reader
pool.hint: Whose feelings are you trying to change?
pool.explain: Reading as the reader shows you where the feeling grows and where it drops.

pool.prompt: Your success criteria have {n} points. How do you know a point is met?
choices: Find the line in your draft that does it
Tick it if you think so
pool.hint: A tick needs proof from the text.
pool.explain: For each of the {n} points, point to the line that meets it. If you cannot find one, that point is missing.

choices: Mum glared and folded her arms
pool.hint: A told line names the feeling. A shown line describes what someone did.
pool.explain: Mum was cross names the feeling. Slamming the pan and glaring show it, so the reader works it out.

pool.prompt: Why can a true line still be wrong for your story?
choices: It may break the effect you want
pool.hint: Think about the cheese sandwich in the ghost story.
pool.explain: A line can be true and still make the reader stop feeling scared or excited. If it breaks the effect, cut or change it.
